title: Avoiding Awkward Silences
summary: We practised starting, continuing and ending conversations with people we don't know well, at parties and conferences. We used tag questions with falling intonation to get people talking, asked questions with the right auxiliary verbs, and learned phrases for changing the topic and closing a conversation politely.

grammar.title: Question tags
grammar.explain: We add a short question (a tag) to the end of a sentence to check something we think is true, or to get someone talking. A positive sentence takes a negative tag, and a negative sentence takes a positive tag. When we are checking, the intonation goes down at the end.
grammar.explain_ar: نضيف سؤالاً قصيراً في آخر الجملة للتأكد من معلومة نظن أنها صحيحة أو لتشجيع الشخص على الكلام. الجملة المثبتة يأتي بعدها سؤال منفي، والجملة المنفية يأتي بعدها سؤال مثبت. نستخدم في السؤال الفعل المساعد نفسه الموجود في الجملة ثم الضمير. وعندما نتأكد من معلومة ينخفض الصوت في نهاية السؤال.
form: Positive sentence + negative tag: You're a friend of Anna's, aren't you?
Negative sentence + positive tag: You aren't from around here, are you?
Tag = the auxiliary verb from the sentence (be / have / do / did / can ...) + pronoun: We have met before, haven't we?
No auxiliary in the sentence? Use do / does / did: He always throws great parties, doesn't he?
Intonation: down at the end when you expect 'yes' (checking); up when it is a real question

examples.en: It's a great party, isn't it?
examples.note: Falling intonation: Jon expects Blanca to agree.

examples.en: You were in the marketing presentation this morning, weren't you?
We met at the conference last year, didn't we?
examples.note: Past simple with no auxiliary → didn't.

examples.en: It's been a busy day, hasn't it?
examples.note: It's been = it has been → hasn't it.

examples.en: I don't think I know you, do I?
You haven't been with the company long, have you?

mistakes.right: You are from Spain, aren't you?
mistakes.why: English uses auxiliary + pronoun, not 'no?' or 'right?'.
The tag uses a pronoun (it), not 'this' or the noun.

mistakes.wrong: He always throws great parties, isn't he?
mistakes.right: He always throws great parties, doesn't he?
mistakes.why: Present simple has no auxiliary, so use does/doesn't.

mistakes.wrong: You aren't from around here, aren't you?
mistakes.right: You aren't from around here, are you?
mistakes.why: A negative sentence needs a positive tag.

quiz.why: 's = is. Positive sentence → negative tag with 'is'.

quiz.q: We met at the conference last year, ___?
quiz.why: Past simple 'met' has no auxiliary, so use 'did'.

quiz.q: You went to university with Ally, ___?

quiz.why: It's been = it has been → hasn't it.

grammar.title: Questions with auxiliary verbs
grammar.explain: To make a question, we usually put an auxiliary verb (do, be or have) before the subject. Use do/does/did with the present and past simple, be with -ing forms and with 'be' sentences, and have with the present perfect.
grammar.explain_ar: لتكوين سؤال نضع عادة فعلاً مساعداً (do أو be أو have) قبل الفاعل. نستخدم do/does مع المضارع البسيط وdid مع الماضي البسيط، ونستخدم be مع صيغة ‎-ing ومع جمل الفعل be، ونستخدم have مع المضارع التام.
form: (Question word) + do / does / did + subject + base verb: What do you do for a living?
(Question word) + am / is / are / was / were + subject: Is this your first visit to Amsterdam?
Have / Has + subject + past participle: Have you lived around here for long?

examples.en: Have you lived around here for long?
What do you do for a living?
examples.note: A polite way to ask about someone's job.

examples.en: Where did you go on holiday last year?
examples.note: Past simple → did + base verb (go, not went).

mistakes.why: Don't forget the auxiliary 'do' before the subject.

mistakes.wrong: Where did you went on holiday?
mistakes.right: Where did you go on holiday?

mistakes.why: There is no other verb, so use 'be' (was).

quiz.q: ___ you lived around here for long?
What ___ you do for a living?
___ this your first visit to Amsterdam?
quiz.why: 'this' is singular and there is no other verb → is.
'your flight' is singular, past, and there is no other verb → was.

quiz.q: Where ___ you go on holiday last year?
quiz.why: Past simple ('last year') with the base verb 'go' → did.
